paras.text: In all the five-year development plans made so far in Pakistan, there were certainly some basic weaknesses and technical faults. Besides this, there are the internal and external reasons — political chaos, drought, the Pakistan–India wars and Afghan refugees etc. — because of which no five-year plan could succeed in achieving its targets. Only the Second Five-Year Plan (1960 to 1965) was crowned with considerable success. However, according to the details of the Economic Survey of Pakistan, during the financial year (2003–2004) there has been an increase in dearness, unemployment, the trade deficit and inflation, while a reduction occurred in foreign loans and an increase in the reserves of foreign exchange. Per-capita income rose from 562 dollars annually to 652 dollars. Moreover the balance of the government’s income and expenditure remained within limits, and the difference has remained only 13 billion rupees, which a few years earlier was up to 76 billion rupees.

3. Making manpower trained.

4. Strengthening the national economy by working on the principle of “self-help”.

5. In view of the importance of the private sector, giving it its due place and making it active for the national economy.

6. Depending as little as possible on foreign aid.

Eighth Five-Year Plan (1993 to 1998)

The basic objectives of the Eighth Five-Year Plan were as follows:

1. Increasing national income by 7 per cent annually.

2. Increasing the agricultural sector by 4.9 per cent annually.

3. Increasing per-capita income by up to twenty-two per cent during the eighth plan.

4. Creating employment opportunities for 6.2 million unemployed individuals.

5. Increasing the proportion of national savings to 19.9%.

6. By the end of the eighth plan, reducing the budget deficit and bringing it equal to 4 per cent of GDP.

7. In this plan, reducing the rate of population growth from 2.9 per cent to 2.7 per cent.

8. Increasing the literacy rate to 48 per cent.

9. Reducing the infant mortality rate from 86 per thousand to 65 per thousand

10. Providing clean drinking water to 70.5 per cent of the population of villages and 95 per cent of the population of cities.

11. Providing basic health facilities at the level of every union council.

Overall review

In all the five-year development plans made so far in Pakistan, there were certainly some basic weaknesses and technical faults. Besides this, there are the internal and external reasons — political chaos, drought, the Pakistan–India wars and Afghan refugees etc. — because of which no five-year plan could succeed in achieving its targets. Only the Second Five-Year Plan (1960 to 1965) was crowned with considerable success. However, according to the details of the Economic Survey of Pakistan, during the financial year (2003–2004) there has been an increase in dearness, unemployment, the trade deficit and inflation, while a reduction occurred in foreign loans and an increase in the reserves of foreign exchange. Per-capita income rose from 562 dollars annually to 652 dollars. Moreover the balance of the government’s income and expenditure remained within limits, and the difference has remained only 13 billion rupees, which a few years earlier was up to 76 billion rupees.

پاکستان میں اب تک جتنے بھی پانچ سالہ ترقیاتی منصوبے بنائے گئے ہیں اُن میں کچھ بنیادی کمزوریاں اور تکنیکی خرابیاں ضرور تھیں۔ اس کے علاوہ سیاسی افراتفری، خشک سالی، پاک بھارت جنگیں اور افغان مہاجرین وغیرہ وہ اندرونی و بیرونی وجوہات ہیں جن کی بنا پر کوئی بھی پانچ سالہ منصوبہ اپنے اہداف حاصل کرنے میں کامیاب نہ ہو سکا۔ صرف دوسرا پانچ سالہ منصوبہ (1960ء تا 1965ء) کافی کامیابی سے ہمکنار رہا۔ تاہم اکنامک سروے آف پاکستان کی تفصیلات کے مطابق (2003ء-2004ء) کے مالی سال کے دوران مہنگائی، بیروزگاری، تجارتی خسارے اور افراطِ زر میں اضافہ ہوا ہے۔ جب کہ بیرونی قرضوں میں کمی واقع ہوئی اور زرِ مبادلہ کے ذخائر میں اضافہ ہوا۔ فی کس آمدنی 562 ڈالر سالانہ سے بڑھ کر 652 ڈالر ہو گئی۔ نیز حکومت کی آمدنی و اخراجات کا توازن حدود میں رہا اور صرف 13 بلین روپے کا فرق رہ گیا ہے۔ جو چند سال پہلے تک 76 بلین روپے تھا۔

3. Making manpower trained.

4. Strengthening the national economy by working on the principle of “self-help”.

5. In view of the importance of the private sector, giving it its due place and making it active for the national economy.

6. Depending as little as possible on foreign aid.

Eighth Five-Year Plan (1993 to 1998)

The basic objectives of the Eighth Five-Year Plan were as follows:

1. Increasing national income by 7 per cent annually.

2. Increasing the agricultural sector by 4.9 per cent annually.

3. Increasing per-capita income by up to twenty-two per cent during the eighth plan.

4. Creating employment opportunities for 6.2 million unemployed individuals.

5. Increasing the proportion of national savings to 19.9%.

6. By the end of the eighth plan, reducing the budget deficit and bringing it equal to 4 per cent of GDP.

7. In this plan, reducing the rate of population growth from 2.9 per cent to 2.7 per cent.

8. Increasing the literacy rate to 48 per cent.

9. Reducing the infant mortality rate from 86 per thousand to 65 per thousand

10. Providing clean drinking water to 70.5 per cent of the population of villages and 95 per cent of the population of cities.

11. Providing basic health facilities at the level of every union council.

Overall review

In all the five-year development plans made so far in Pakistan, there were certainly some basic weaknesses and technical faults. Besides this, there are the internal and external reasons — political chaos, drought, the Pakistan–India wars and Afghan refugees etc. — because of which no five-year plan could succeed in achieving its targets. Only the Second Five-Year Plan (1960 to 1965) was crowned with considerable success. However, according to the details of the Economic Survey of Pakistan, during the financial year (2003–2004) there has been an increase in dearness, unemployment, the trade deficit and inflation, while a reduction occurred in foreign loans and an increase in the reserves of foreign exchange. Per-capita income rose from 562 dollars annually to 652 dollars. Moreover the balance of the government’s income and expenditure remained within limits, and the difference has remained only 13 billion rupees, which a few years earlier was up to 76 billion rupees.
